Today through Thursday...

Very warm conditions persist this afternoon, with high 
temperatures forecast to reach into the 80s to low 90sF (warmest 
in eastern MT). Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms 
are forecast this afternoon. There is a Marginal Risk for isolated
strong to scattered thunderstorms this afternoon over west-
central Montana. For our area, this includes Musselshell, Golden 
Valley, and Wheatland Counties. The primary concerns with any 
storms today are erratic wind gusts up to 50 mph and heavy 
rainfall. Within the Marginal Risk area, the threats include wind 
gusts up to 60 mph and hail. The risk for stronger to severe 
storms is limited by weak forcing and minimal shear across the 
forecast area. HiRes models show inverted V soundings over the 
west-central areas through 500mb further showing the risk for 
potentially strong wind gusts with any activity. The eastern 
counties have much better instability with 1000-1800 J/kg of 
surface CAPE and slightly better bulk shear. The breezy ESE winds 
over the eastern areas will continue into this evening, before 
diminishing with increasing precipitation chances. There is a 
defined area of convergence and weak frontogenesis shown by 
mesoanalysis over Sheridan, Rosebud, Custer, and Powder River 
Counties this afternoon. Current radar and satellite analysis 
show showers and thunderstorms over the Bighorns, models depict 
further activity developing over the area of convergence.

Additional concerns with any activity this afternoon and evening 
will be with the recent burn scars including the Elk, Robertson 
Draw, and the East Side Fires. Otherwise, the risk of flooding 
remains low across the area.

An upper low over the Great Basin will continue its track 
northward into Wyoming on Saturday. This will bring widespread 
rainfall and thunderstorms, as well as the threat for a few strong
to severe thunderstorms in southeast Montana. A surface low is 
expected to develop over northeast WY, western SD, and far 
southeast MT. Counties including and east of Yellowstone County 
are covered by another Marginal Risk (1/5) for isolated strong to 
severe thunderstorms. The location of the upper low will play a 
big hand in where stronger storms are able to develop. Currently 
models depict the best area of upper divergence over southern MT 
where decent ample forcing along with long skinny CAPE (up to 1000
J/kg) and steep lapse rates (>7.5 C/km) exists. Note, the best 
parameters within the Marginal exists along the Dakotas border. It
will be tricky to determine the evolution of strong to severe 
thunderstorms given morning convection. Although models do show a 
break into the afternoon down there, allowing for temperatures to 
warm and instability to rebound. The primary threats are strong 
wind gusts up to 60 mph, hail up to quarter size, and heavy 
rainfall. While the risk is very low for tornadoes, there is a 
caveat to this. Depending on the location of the surface low and 
the movement of a boundary over western SD, there is a brief 
window of tornadic potential near the low in the warm sector, in 
far southeast Montana along US-212 in Carter County.

There is a moderate to high chance for at least 0.5" of rainfall 
across the region through Monday. For areas west and south of 
Miles City the chance for at least an inch of rainfall is moderate
to high. The latest forecast depicts this. The chance for an inch
is lower in the southeast, including Fallon, Powder River, 
Carter, and Sheridan Counties. Because of the widespread rainfall 
and the threat for heavy rainfall, Flash Flood Watches have been 
issued for the Elk, Robertson Draw, and the East Side Fire, 
Saturday morning through Saturday evening. There is a Slight Risk 
(2/4) for excessive rainfall central MT tomorrow. This corresponds
to the latest HREF 1"/hr rainfall probabilities of 40-70% for a 
point within 25km. While the risk for flooding remains low overall
at this time, there could be localized concerns due to near 
stationary thunderstorms and heavy rainfall on the mentioned burn 
scars. People near burn scars and flood prone areas should be 
alert and think about a plan if flooding or debris flows occur. 

A cold front is depicted moving through Saturday night, allowing 
for much of the thunderstorm activity to move into the Dakotas. 
The upper low has other plans though, with ensembles showing it 
phasing with an upper trough over the PNW. The presence of cooler 
air will bring snow levels down from 11kft to around 9kt by Sunday
morning. Additional showers and weak thunderstorms will linger 
through Monday, though severe weather is not expected at this 
time. For the mountains, snowfall above 9kft is forecast, with 
several inches of accumulations above 10kft. The majority of 
accumulating snowfall is forecast on Sunday, diminishing into 
Monday morning. Be prepared for potential impacts to the Beartooth
Highway this weekend.
